newsitem.title: peru: Fujimori popularity takes hit as siege drags on.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori popularity takes hit as siege drags on.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori's popularity fell slightly in polls released on Monday as Peruvians feared the holding of 72 hostages by Marxist rebels at the Japanese ambassador's house could drag on for months.
Fujimori's approval rating fell four percentage points during March to 48 percent in the first week of April, according to a survey by leading pollster Apoyo published in Monday's papers.
Six out of 10 respondents said they thought the hostage situation could go on for another one to three months or even more, according to the poll of 512 adults living in Lima.

The low point in expectations and the drop in Fujimori's popularity came as negotiators clamped a virtual news blackout on talks with Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels holed up in the diplomatic mansion with the hostages.
"We are in a stage of (giving out) very little information," chief negotiator Juan Luis Cipriani, Roman Catholic Archbishop of Ayacucho, said on Sunday. But he added talks "go on advancing."

Meanwhile, military authorities told reporters mounting a 24-hour watch on the residence to remove their cameras from a corner 100 yards (metres) from the entrance. They said that would free vehicles' access to the area. They would not elaborate.

Cipriani and two other mediators have been carrying on an almost daily shuttle diplomacy between the government and Nestor Cerpa, the MRTA leader who led some 20 fighters into the residence on Dec. 17 while Japanese Ambassador Morihisa Aoki was throwing a bash for 500 dignitaries.

They later released most, keeping only 72 men, including Aoki, Bolivian Ambassador Jorge Gumucio, two Peruvian cabinet ministers and two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen. The MRTA has demanded the release of 450 jailed comrades in exchange for the hostages, a demand Fujimori publicly vowed he will never bow to.

But sources close to the negotiations said the two sides were discreetly discussing a possible compromise settlement that could include leniency for low-ranking MRTA prisoners or release of those detained but not convicted.

The opinion poll showed seven out of 10 Peruvians oppose freeing even those MRTA inmates convicted of minor crimes, but an equal number said they favoured negotiations, with only 15 percent proposing that troops be sent in to free the hostages.

No margin of error was given for the Apoyo survey, but commentators pointed out it was taken before an unrelated scandal involving the killing and torture of army intelligence agents, which could further harm the government's image.
